en: I will take his craftsmen as booty
And make him taste my salt!
When you travel back from there,
He summers in Eki-Kemin,
Tethers a pair of black horses,
Makes the dense forest his livestock,
And the black cave his home;
He sharpens his eloquent tongue
And speaks before the khan—
Hero Ürbü, the bald Eybit.
He knows the tongues of seventy tribes,
A fully accomplished orator.
He gathered kites and made them hunting birds.
He gathered mixed clans and made a people.
He gathered stray birds and made hunting birds;
He gathered wanderers and made a people.
Once poor, he became rich;
Once alone, he became numerous.
Give hero Ürbü my greetings.
Tell him to come to my feast
And see this spectacle.
If he does not come to my feast,
If he does not see this spectacle,
If I should take him into my wrath,
I will turn back and raid him
And beat out his old madness.
On this side of there
Are Khan Tekechi, Khan Shygay,
And Zhamgyrchy of the Eshtek—
The peoples of three khans lie side by side.
Their stock is Kyrgyz, their sons true;
Give all three khans my greetings.
Say Kökötöy's many livestock
Have filled Ükürchü;
Say they surpass the Muslim peoples;
Say they dug cooking pits
Along Üch-Kapkak.
Say that Bokmurun, Kökötöy's son,
Has camped at Üch-Karkyra;
Say that Kökötöy's countless riches
Have filled the face of the earth,
And the time has come to give the feast!
Tell them to come to my feast
And heed my words.
If they do not come to my feast,
Tell them to behold Kökötöy's thousand champions
From atop their own houses!
Dwelling in Wide Ili,
They are imposing heroes.
The two khans Edigey and Teyish—
There, as we can see,
Lie Muslims beyond counting.
Give those two my greetings;
Tell them to come to my feast
And see with their own eyes
Kökötöy's great prize.
If they do not heed my words,
If they remain away from my feast,
I will take and slaughter their mares as booty;
I will bind and seize their foot soldiers,
Make them shoulder and carry firewood,
And thus settle their account.
Those who answer me defiantly—
I will punch out their brains.
When you go farther on,
You will see another young man,
In the broad valley of Sary-Arka,
Sprawled imposingly there—
The champion of the Kazakhs.
He husks his millet, stones and all;
He praises his wife like a maiden.
His lattice walls are of wood,
And his elder brother is of the Alach.
Hero Kökchö, son of Aydar Khan—
Who has ever stood beside me!
The heel of the blue boot,
Convey my many greetings
To Aydar Khan's Kökchö.
Dwelling in Sary-Arka,
Tethering his piebald-yellow herd,
No enemy went against him in combat.
His manner and conduct are brusque—
Poor lord Kökchö of the Kazakhs.
Kökchö, khan of the Kazakhs,
Give Khan Kökchö my greetings.
At Kökötöy's memorial feast,
The people gather in a seething mass,
Swarming like black insects;
To Khan Kökötöy's memorial feast,
To the edge of the vast gathering,
To his dark-bay piebald banner,
To the tumult of the assembled Chinese,
Along the Karkyra,
To Khan Kökötöy's feast,
Heroes and lions will come;
Unbeliever and Muslim,
All alike will come, none remaining.
The spear-points will glitter;
The ground will heave, filled with people.
The multitude will come seething;
Their numbers will resemble a black swarm.
If you do not come to this feast,
If you do not see this spectacle,
Say he will raise an uproar
And take not only the Kazakhs' horses
But their cattle as well!
When you pass beyond there,
Traveling still farther,
When you reach Kakan-Chyn,
There are the Manchu and Kalmyk peoples;
There is the hero you must tell.
Khan Zholoy of the Kalmyks—
Tell him to put on his karapchy,
Mount Achbuudan,
And drive his people
To Üch-Karkyra,
To Khan Kökötöy's feast;
Let him arrange his own order.
For this feast of Kökötöy,
Let no one among his people remain;
Let the Kalmyks, numerous as cow hairs,
With great Zholoy, their great champion,
Drive forth all together;
Among those Kalmyks,
Let not one remain apart.
For seven years he traveled on foot
And greased his accomplished spear;
He slew seventy men—
Hero Zholoy, reeking of demons.
For sixty years he traveled on foot,
Fighting and greasing his spear;
He slew sixty men—
Hero Zholoy, reeking of blood.
Tell him to put on his great boots
And mount his great racehorse.
Tell him to see this spectacle
And come to my feast!
If he does not see this spectacle,
If he does not come to my feast,
Taking seven standard-banners,
Taking a road across the land,
Taking a host that makes the earth sag,
I will beat out his raging madness,
Raid Khan Zholoy,
And cause three great tumults.
I will raid away not merely the Kalmyks' horses,
But their entire herd.
If Zholoy heeds the command, tell him to come;
If that Zholoy will not heed it,
Tell him to behold Kökötöy's red banner with its golden crescent
From above his own blood!
When you go beyond there,
Along the river that flows backward,
There, taking shape in the haze,
Rising indistinctly to a point,
The Chinese gave it a curious name:
They call it Tash-Köpürö.
Dwelling in Tash-Köpürö
Are the renowned Sibe people.
The formidable champion of the Sibe
Is called Great Ylama.
They have peoples of many kinds;
If we told of them, there are many.
The Sibe people's custom is this:
When a young wife gives birth,
From the reed that cut its navel cord,
They call the child's clan Sibe;
If it happens to remain until dusk,
Wolves tear it apart and eat it.
Go all the way to the Lama and tell him,
Say he must come to this feast of mine,
Kökötöy's festivities—
Say the buried Shibee must see them!
If he does not heed these words of mine,
If he does not consent to what I say,
If he does not come to this feast of mine,
I will slaughter and destroy his people
And leave them to the wolves.
I will shatter those of his people who remain
And drive them away on foot in misery.
When you travel farther on,
There is a gray and misty desert;
Upon the face of that desert
There is a people called the Soloon.
They lock themselves in at night;
They have walls built to bar the way.
The ruler of those Soloon
Is a khan named Orokkyr.
If you ask what the Soloon are like,
Their heads are long like mortars;
Spread across their backs,
They have hair like a pestle shaft.
Their entire wretched custom
Is to roast and eat snakes, scorpions, and lizards,
And any frogs they find
Out on the steppe.
Their khan is Orokkyr;
Take word to Orokkyr.
Say every one of those people
Who live like livestock must come;
Say they must see Kökötöy's festive feast
At Karkyra.
Say Kökötöy's son Bokmurun
Has moved here from Tashkent,
Say he has camped at Üch-Karkyra,
Say Kökötöy's great wealth
Has filled the face of the earth.
Say he must come to this feast of mine;
If he does not come to this feast of mine,
Say Kökötöy's countless spear-bearing champions
Will appear directly above him!
I will overrun and slaughter his people,
And leave them wearing black headdresses in mourning.
When you travel farther on,
There are the mines of Altyn-Too;
If one kept telling of Beijing,
Its tales would never end.
Its city, called Bakburchun in Chinese—
I know much about those people.
They raise a haze over the steppe;
They have buildings made into towers.
The Manchu khan Ezkara
Is another extraordinary hero.
He has a scroll bearing a great rank,
And a horse like Chongküröng.
Those who hear his fame take fright;
He saddles that bay horse.
The sixty Manchu burku
I will hang—
He studied foreign learning for six years.
His courage is of another order,
A peerless champion born among the Manchus.
Both a judge of horses and a warrior,
That lion is the lion you must name.
Say Ezkara, khan of the Manchus,
Must consent to these words of mine.
Say not a soul from the Manchu people must remain behind,
But all must come to Karkyra
For Kökötöy's memorial feast.
Say they must see Kökötöy's many festivities
Before their own eyes.
Say the Manchu baldheads who carry stones
Must come;
Say the strong men of the coat-wearing Chinese
Must come!
With their gauntlets put on,
Let not one of the Kalday remain.
I have honored them with an invitation to the feast;
Hey, Ezkara, hear this!
Kökötöy's livestock left at his death,
The treasure filling forty rooms—
I will open the treasure-house,
And for each honored chief who comes,
I will scatter him his share.
Say he must come to this feast of mine,
Say he must see these festivities!
